title: Measuring a good split
objectives: Compute Gini impurity and entropy for a split.
Choose a split by the weighted drop in impurity.

screens.title: Two splits, one score
screens.prose: A node holds 40 loans: 20 defaults and 20 repaid. Two candidate splits, A and B, divide it in different ways. Each side predicts its majority, as in lesson 1.
screens.question: How many of the 40 loans does split B misclassify?

widget.label: Loans split B gets wrong
widget.accept: 10 exactly: the 10 defaults on B's left side, which predicts repaid.

hints.text: On each side, the loans outside the majority are the mistakes.
B's left side has 10 D and 20 R, so it predicts repaid.
Left: 10 defaults are wrong. Right: 10 D and 0 R, no mistakes. Total 10.

feedback.correct: Ten, the same as split A: 5 + 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the minority on each side of B and add.

byKey.twenty: You counted the 20 repaid loans as mistakes. B's left side predicts repaid, so its 10 defaults are the mistakes.
byKey.zero: B's right side is pure, but its left side still mixes 10 defaults with 20 repaid.

explain.text: Split B gets 10 wrong, and so does A (5 on each side). Yet B leaves a pure node of 10 defaults that needs no more work. Counting mistakes cannot tell the two splits apart; we need a finer score.

screens.title: A finer score
screens.prose: Score a node by its mix. If a share $p_D$ defaulted and $p_R$ repaid, use $$G = 1 - p_D^2 - p_R^2.$$ A pure node scores 0; a 50-50 node scores the most. This is the **Gini impurity**.
screens.question: What is $G$ for A's left side, 15 D and 5 R?

widget.label: Gini impurity of 15 D and 5 R

hints.text: Find the two shares first: 15 of 20 and 5 of 20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each share, add the squares, and subtract from 1.

byKey.nosq: You subtracted the shares without squaring them. The shares always add to 1, so that gives 0 for every node.
byKey.err: That is the error rate, the minority share. Gini squares the shares: $1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2$.
byKey.sumsq: That is $p_D^2 + p_R^2$. Gini is 1 minus it.

explain.text: $1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375$. By symmetry A's right side, 5 D and 15 R, also scores 0.375. $G$ is the chance that two loans drawn from the node at random have different outcomes.

screens.title: Two impurity curves
screens.prose: Here is $G$ against the default share $p$, beside a second score, **entropy** $H = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)$, in bits. The dashed line is the error rate. Slide $p$.
screens.question: Read the entropy at $p = 0.2$, in bits.

hints.text: Move the slider to 0.20 and read the caption.
The entropy curve is the top one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $p$ to 0.20 and read the entropy, not the Gini.

byKey.gini: 0.32 is the Gini value at 0.2. Entropy is the higher curve.
byKey.half: That is the peak at $p = 0.5$. Move the slider to 0.20.

explain.text: Both curves are 0 at a pure node and peak at $p = \tfrac12$: Gini at 0.5, entropy at 1 bit. Both are curved, unlike the error rate, so they reward a side that gets purer even when its majority does not change.

screens.title: Weigh each side
screens.prose: A split's score is the **weighted** impurity of its sides: each side's Gini times its share of the loans. Fill the table for both splits, then name the better one.
screens.question: Fill in the missing cells.

hints.text: Weighted Gini = (left loans / 40) × left Gini + (right loans / 40) × right Gini.
B left has 10 D and 20 R: $p_D = \tfrac13$, so $G = 1 - \tfrac19 - \tfrac49$.
B left: $\tfrac49 = 0.444$. B right is pure: 0. Weighted: $\tfrac{30}{40} \times 0.444 = 0.333$, below A's 0.375.

feedback.correct: B scores 0.333 against A's 0.375, so B is better.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each side's Gini by its share of the 40 loans, then pick the lower weighted score.

explain.text: A: $0.5 \times 0.375 + 0.5 \times 0.375 = 0.375$. B: $0.75 \times 0.444 + 0.25 \times 0 = 0.333$. The drop from the parent's 0.5 is the split's **gain**: 0.125 for A, 0.167 for B.

screens.title: The tiny pure side
screens.prose: Split C peels off one loan: its left side is 1 D, 0 R, and its right side is 19 D, 20 R. A colleague averages the two Gini values: C scores $\tfrac{0 + 0.500}{2} = 0.25$, below A's 0.375.
screens.question: Which split should the tree prefer?

options.text: A: weighted by size, C scores 0.487 against A's 0.375
C: its average impurity, 0.25, is lower
options.why: You averaged the sides as if they were the same size. C's pure side holds 1 loan; its other 39 are as mixed as the parent.

options.text: Neither: both have one side better than the parent
options.why: Only A purifies both sides. C's big side is barely purer than the parent's 0.5.

options.text: C: a pure side always wins
options.why: A pure side of one loan buys almost nothing. What counts is how many loans end up purer.

hints.text: How many loans sit on each side of C?
C's right side holds 39 of the 40 loans, with Gini 0.500.
Weighted: $\tfrac{1}{40} \times 0 + \tfrac{39}{40} \times 0.4997 = 0.487$. A scores 0.375.

feedback.correct: Weighting shows C barely helps: its gain is 0.013 against A's 0.125.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each side by its share of the loans before comparing.

byKey.c: You compared impurities without weighting by group size. One pure loan cannot outweigh 39 mixed ones.

explain.text: Weighted, C scores $\tfrac{39}{40} \times 0.4997 = 0.487$, a gain of only 0.013. A gains 0.125. Always weight a side by its share of the parent's rows.

screens.title: A gain that accuracy cannot see
screens.prose: A node holds 30 defaults and 10 repaid, so it predicts default and gets 10 wrong. A split sends 18 defaults left and the other 22 loans, 12 D and 10 R, right.
screens.question: Both sides still predict default, so mistakes stay at 10. What is the Gini gain?

hints.text: Parent Gini first: $p_D = 0.75$.

feedback.correct: A gain of 0.102, while the mistake count does not move.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the weighted child Gini from the parent's 0.375.

byKey.zero: That is the gain in accuracy: 10 mistakes before and after. Gini sees that 18 loans are now settled for sure.
byKey.unw: You averaged the two sides without weighting. The right side holds 22 of the 40 loans.

explain.text: Accuracy sees no change, so a tree that split on accuracy would stop here. Gini sees 18 settled loans and a 12-10 node that the next question can work on. That is why trees split on impurity, not accuracy.

screens.title: Three rating buckets
screens.prose: The formulas never assumed two classes. A node of 20 bonds holds 10 rated A, 6 BBB and 4 BB. Gini sums a square for every class: $G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$.
screens.question: What is the Gini impurity of this node?

hints.text: Shares first: 10, 6 and 4 out of 20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square all three shares and subtract their sum from 1.

byKey.sumsq: That is $\sum_k p_k^2$. Gini is 1 minus it.
byKey.two: 0.5 is the most two classes can reach. With three classes the ceiling is $\tfrac23$.

explain.text: $1 - 0.25 - 0.09 - 0.04 = 0.62$. With $K$ classes Gini peaks at $1 - \tfrac1K$ and entropy at $\log_2 K$ bits, here 0.667 and 1.585. Splits are scored exactly as before.

screens.title: Gain, in general
screens.prose: For a split of $n$ rows into $n_L$ left and $n_R$ right, with impurity $I$: $$\text{gain} = I(\text{parent}) - \tfrac{n_L}{n} I(L) - \tfrac{n_R}{n} I(R).$$ With entropy, the gain is called **information gain**. scikit-learn uses Gini unless you pass `criterion="entropy"`.
screens.question: Split A sends 20 loans each way, and each side has entropy 0.811. What is A's information gain? The parent's entropy is 1.

hints.text: Both sides weigh one half.
Weighted child entropy: $0.5 \times 0.811 + 0.5 \times 0.811 = 0.811$.

feedback.correct: 0.189 bits for A; B gains 0.311, so entropy also prefers B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the weighted child entropy from 1.

byKey.sum: You subtracted 0.811 without weighting each side by one half: $1 - 0.811$, not $2 - 2 \times 0.811$.
byKey.child: 0.811 is the weighted child entropy. The gain is the drop from the parent's 1.

explain.text: A gains 0.189 bits and B 0.311, the same order as Gini's 0.125 and 0.167. The two curves have nearly the same shape, so they nearly always choose the same split.

screens.title: Gini and entropy in code
screens.prose: Turn the two formulas into functions of a node's class counts. Shares with a count of 0 add nothing to entropy, so skip them: $0 \log_2 0$ is taken as 0.
screens.question: Complete `gini` and `entropy`. Each returns its value rounded to 6 places.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: two classes, three and four classes, pure nodes and an empty node. Each value is compared with math.isclose.

hints.text: Turn each count into a share `c / n` first.
Gini: `1 - sum((c / n) ** 2 for c in counts)`.
Entropy: `-sum(c / n * log2(c / n) for c in counts if c > 0)`.

feedback.correct: Both scores match the curves you read.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Skip zero counts in entropy, and square the shares in Gini.

byKey.test-9: `log2(0)` raises an error. Skip classes with a count of 0, as the `if c > 0` filter does.

explain.text: A four-way even split has entropy 2 bits: you need two yes-or-no answers to name the class. That is the sense in which entropy measures surprise.

screens.title: The gain of a split
screens.prose: Now score a whole split from the labels on each side. `impurity(labels, criterion)` is written for you. You add the weighting.
screens.question: Complete `split_gain`: the parent's impurity minus the weighted impurity of the sides, rounded to 6 places.

hints.text: Weight each side by its number of rows over `n`.
`len(y_left) * impurity(y_left, criterion)` is the left side's share times its impurity, times `n`.
`child = (len(y_left) * impurity(y_left, criterion) + len(y_right) * impurity(y_right, criterion)) / n`.

feedback.correct: Your gains match scikit-learn's at the root of the 12-loan tree: 0.209921 with Gini.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Weight each side's impurity by its number of rows, divide by `n`, and pass `criterion` through.

byKey.test-4: Split C should gain only 0.012821. If you got about 0.25, the sides were averaged without weights.

explain.text: An empty side has weight 0, so a split that moves no rows gains exactly 0. At the 12-loan root, *leverage ≤ 3* gains 0.209921 with Gini, the largest of any split, which is why scikit-learn chose it.

screens.title: The best split, by search
screens.prose: Put it together: try every feature and every midpoint, and keep the largest Gini gain. `impurity(labels)` is loaded. Keep the first best found when two tie.
screens.question: Complete `best_split(X, y)`, returning `(feature, threshold, gain)`.

hints.text: Split the labels by `v <= t`, as in lesson 1.
Gain is `impurity(y)` minus the weighted impurity of `left` and `right`.
Then `if g > best[2]: best = (f, t, g)`. Strict `>` keeps the first best on a tie.

feedback.correct: Your search finds the same root splits as scikit-learn.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Weight the sides by their sizes, and replace `best` only on a strictly larger gain.

byKey.test-3: Both features split these rows perfectly. Strict `>` keeps feature 0, found first.
byKey.test-5: A pure node gains nothing from any split, so `best` should stay `(None, None, 0.0)`.

screens.title: A market-regime classifier
screens.prose: A desk labels 200 trading days risk-on (120) or risk-off (80). A tree's first split is *realised volatility above 20%?* Below it: 105 on, 15 off. Above it: 15 on, 65 off.
screens.question: What is the Gini gain of this split?

widget.label: Gini gain of the volatility split

hints.text: Parent: 80 off of 200, so $p = 0.4$ and $G = 0.48$.

feedback.correct: A gain of 0.227: nearly half the parent's 0.48.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the three Gini values, weight the sides by 120 and 80 days, and subtract.

byKey.child: 0.253 is the weighted impurity left after the split. The gain is how far it fell from 0.48.
byKey.unw: You averaged the sides equally. The calm side holds 120 of the 200 days, so it weighs 0.6.

explain.text: The split removes 0.227 of the parent's 0.48, about 47% of the impurity. The gain measures how much the question tells you about the regime. A momentum split gaining 0.01 would say almost nothing.

ideas: Counting mistakes is too blunt: two splits can make the same mistakes while one leaves a pure node.
Gini $1 - \sum p_k^2$ and entropy $-\sum p_k \log_2 p_k$ are 0 when pure, peak at an even mix and nearly always rank splits the same way.
A split's gain is the parent's impurity minus the size-weighted impurity of its sides; the tree takes the largest.

formula.name: Gain of a split
formula.note: With entropy it is the information gain.

summary.trap: Averaging the sides' impurities without weighting by size, which makes a one-row pure side look good.

quiz.question: What is the weighted Gini of the two sides?

quiz.question: What is the Gini gain of this split?

options.text: 0: the right side is the parent itself
The parent's whole impurity: the empty side is pure
options.why: An empty side has weight 0, so its purity counts for nothing.

options.text: Negative: an empty side is worse than none
options.why: Gain is never negative for Gini or entropy. Here it is exactly 0.

feedback.correct: Zero gain: the split changed nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What are the two sides' weights?

explain.text: The right side holds all $n$ rows with the parent's impurity, weight 1; the empty left side has weight 0. Gain $= I - 1 \times I - 0 = 0$.

quiz.prose: You fit `DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)` and later the same with `criterion="entropy"`.
quiz.question: What do you expect?

options.text: The same or nearly the same splits: both curves rise and fall together
Very different trees, since entropy can exceed 1
options.why: Entropy's scale is larger, but the split that lowers one score most nearly always lowers the other most.
Entropy is an impurity, curved like Gini. Neither counts mistakes.

feedback.correct: Gini is the default, and the two rarely disagree.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the shapes of the two curves on screen 3.

explain.text: Both are 0 when pure, peak at $p = \tfrac12$ and are curved. On splits A and B they gave the same ranking. When they differ, the gains are usually close.

byKey.third: $\tfrac13$ is $\sum p_k^2$. Gini is 1 minus it.
